output:
Kelechi,

Yes, I actually did it. You said put it in writing, so here it is in writing, on paper, in an envelope, with a stamp. I hope you're reading this on the train like you said you would, and I hope the person next to you is wondering why you're smiling at a letter like it's 1997.

I'm going to try not to preach, because I know you. The minute you smell a sermon you start nodding and saying "true, true" while your mind is somewhere else. So I'll just tell you what I think and you can argue with me after.

At my birthday you were moaning about work again. Don't deny it. Nine years at that firm and every time I see you, it's the same story: same spreadsheet, same costings, same meetings about why the other people's numbers don't add up. You said it like a joke but it didn't sound like a joke. And on your own birthday you said, "I just want to do something that matters before 40." I remember because you said it right after the cake, and it killed the mood small. You're 34. That gives you six years. I'm just doing the maths, since that's my job.

So this is me being serious. Come and teach maths.

Before you laugh, hear me out properly.

**You've been doing it for free since Moremi.**

Abeg, have you forgotten? Further maths, A. And the week before exams, half the hostel was in your room with their textbooks while you explained things on the back of whatever paper you could find. People who had been avoiding the subject all semester suddenly found their way to your door. I was one of them, I'm not too proud to say it. You never made anybody feel stupid. You'd explain it once, then again another way, then a third way, and you'd crack a joke somewhere in the middle so the person didn't feel bad for still not getting it. That isn't a small skill. Most people who are good at maths can't do it. They get impatient, or they explain it the way their own brain sees it and wonder why you're not following. You've never been like that.

And then Christmas. My nephew still talks about the jollof rice. You sat that boy down with plates and portions and taught him fractions with rice. Half a plate, a quarter of a plate, "if I take two quarters from you, how much is left?" He's still telling people about it. His teacher has probably been on fractions with him for a year and he can't tell you one thing she said, but he remembers the rice. That's what I mean. You were born for this, and instead you're checking other people's costings in Croydon. It's a waste, Kelechi. I'm saying it with love, but it's a waste.

**We actually need you.**

This isn't just me wanting my friend in the staffroom (although I do, it would be nice to have someone to laugh with at break). My school has 1,100 kids. Since September, two of our Year 9 maths groups have been covered by a supply teacher. Nothing against him, he's trying, but he's not permanent and the kids know it. Every school round here is short of maths teachers. You wouldn't be one more person in a queue. You'd be the person they're desperate for.

**Let me tell you about Damola.**

Last month I had a Year 11 boy, Damola, who'd been fighting simultaneous equations for three weeks. Three weeks. I tried everything. He was frustrated, I was frustrated, he'd started doing that thing where they say "I'm just not a maths person." Then one Tuesday it clicked. Mid-lesson he looked at his book, looked at me, and shouted, "IS THAT ALL??" The whole class started clapping. Actually clapping. For simultaneous equations. He was grinning like he'd scored at Wembley.

I went home that day and couldn't stop thinking about it. Tell me honestly when your spreadsheet last made you feel like that. I'll wait.

**Now the bad parts, because I won't lie to you.**

I know if I only tell you the sweet side you won't believe a word, so here it is.

It's hard. Some days are very hard. The marking never finishes. You think you're done and there's another pile. Behaviour some days is proper wahala. There are lessons where you've planned everything and one boy decides today is the day, and the whole thing goes sideways, and you just have to manage it and start again tomorrow.

When I started in 2019, I cried in the car park twice in my first term. Twice. Sitting in my car with my lanyard still on, crying, then wiping my face and driving home. I'm telling you because I want you to know exactly what you're walking into. The first year will humble you.

But it gets better. It really does. You learn the kids, they learn you, you build your systems, you stop taking everything personally. I don't cry in the car park anymore. These days the car park is where I sit for five minutes laughing at something a Year 8 said.

**The money.**

I know this is where your quantity surveyor brain is going, so let me address it. Yes, your pay will drop in the first year. I'm not going to pretend it won't. But the route I'm talking about is the salaried one, so you're paid while you train. You won't be going back to being a broke student eating Indomie. It's one year of training, and you'd start September 2027. After that it goes up, and it keeps going up. The pension is solid, and I know you, you'll appreciate a good pension more than you'll admit. And the holidays, Kelechi. I'm not saying you won't be marking in some of them, but you'll have actual time. Time to travel, time to rest, time to visit your mum without begging HR for five days off.

Run the numbers properly over ten years, not just one. You're the costings man, you know how to do that.

**"I'm too old."**

I know you're thinking it. Stop. A woman in my department started at 41. Forty-one. She's one of the best teachers we have, and the kids respect her because she's had a whole other life and they can tell. At 34 you're a baby in teacher years. You'd walk in with nine years of real-world experience, managing budgets, dealing with difficult clients, explaining numbers to people who don't want to hear them. Do you know how useful that is in a classroom? When a Year 10 asks "when am I ever going to use this?" you can actually answer them.

**So here's what I'm asking.**

I'm not asking you to quit tomorrow, and I'm not asking you to sign anything. Just come to the open evening.

**Thursday 19 November, 6pm, at the training partnership in Lewisham.**

That's it. One evening. You go, you listen, you ask your hundred questions (I know you'll have a hundred questions), and if you leave thinking "no, this isn't for me," fine. I'll never mention it again. Well, I'll mention it maybe once a year at your birthday, but that's it.

I'll come with you. I'll meet you there, or we'll go together, whichever you want. Afterwards we can get food and you can tell me all the reasons it's a bad idea, and I'll listen. I promise.

Applications for next September open soon, so this is the time. If you wait until "next year" you'll still be on the same spreadsheet in 2028, telling me the same story at my next birthday, and I'll have to post you another letter. Neither of us wants that. Stamps are expensive.

You're patient, you're funny, and you explain things without making people feel small. Kids would love you, I'm telling you now. They'd be doing impressions of you within a week, and that's how you'd know they liked you.

You said you wanted to do something that matters before 40. This could be it. Come and have a look.

Text me when you've finished reading. And don't just send "lol."

Your guy from Moremi,

[your name]

P.S. If you show this letter to anyone at work, tell them I said hello and that I'm stealing you.
